newsitem.title: GERMANY: Scrap Eurofighter, say Germany's Greens.
newsitem.headline: Scrap Eurofighter, say Germany's Greens.

text.p: The opposition Greens party on Tuesday urged the German government withdraw from the controversial Eurofighter combat jet project, calling it a relic of Cold War thinking which the cash-strapped administration could ill afford.

In a parliamentary motion, the Greens, who could end up after next year's general election in a "red-green" coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, said spending 23 billion marks ($13.2 billion) on the four-nation project was not justified.

"It is already clear the Eurofighter will become Germany's most expensive and superfluous arms project since the war," Angelika Beer and Winfried Nachtwei, who represent the Greens on parliament's defence committee, said in a joint statement.
Calling Eurofighter "a financial time bomb", the Greens said buying 180 of the jets made no sense since it was conceived to counter a Soviet military threat which no longer existed.

The Greens motion called on the lower house of parliament to urge Bonn to pull out the Eurofighter and instead focus its efforts on achieving regional disarmament via the Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

In reply, the current centre-right coalition's junior partner, the Christian Social Union (CSU), said the Eurofighter was vital for maintaining Germany's credibility within the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

CSU chief whip Eduard Oswald said quitting Eurofighter would jeopardise an entire industry and "be a slap in the face for many qualified workers who would lose their jobs". Around 18,000 jobs, many in the CSU's Bavarian heartland, hang on the fate of Eurofighter.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and Finance Minister Theo Waigel are due to hold more talks this week on the 1998 defence budget, and want to find one billion marks to pay for startup production for the Eurofighter. Project partners Britain, Italy and Spain are anxiously awaiting the outcome.

Waigel is also talking to Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA), the project's German partner, to claw back another billion marks in pre-financing for DASA's civilian Airbus operations to ensure Eurofighter production can start.

Ruehe, speaking in Dresden, told reporters that a final decision would only be made by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on next year's defence budget on July 11, and he gave assurances provision would be made to buy Eurofighter.

He said there was still room for savings in small-scale defence projects, but added that Germany's 340,000-strong army would be spared spending cuts to help pay for Eurofighter. Separately, the Defence Ministry said it may have to delay buying other military hardware over the next few years to make room to pay for the Eurofighter.
But a spokesman dismissed as incorrect a newspaper report which said on Tuesday that Bonn had already decided which items would have to be struck from the ministry's shopping list.
The regional Flensburger Tageblatt newspaper said that the Defence Ministry had decided to delay the purchase of the EGV supply ship to 2002, saving 320 million marks.
"A few projects will have to be spun out," the spokesman told Reuters, adding no decisions have yet been taken.
Dietrich Austermann, budget spokesman for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), also said the EGV should not fall victim to the drive to buy Eurofighter.
"It is not acceptable that one defence project falls victim to another," he told Reuters. "But I am optimistic that we can buy both the ship and the aircraft."
And Juergen Koppelin, budget spokesman for coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said he would not support buying Eurofighter if the EGV is put on ice.
"Without the EGV the Eurofighter just won't happen, even though the Eurofighter is militarily necessary," he was quoted by the newspaper as saying.
